title: Building Scikit-learn Pipelines
summary: As your workflow grows, doing preprocessing steps manually becomes error-prone, and scikit-learn pipelines solve this by chaining every step, scaling, encoding, and the model, into a single object. This matters most for preventing data leakage, one o

# Building Scikit-learn Pipelines ##### The model that scored 0.94 in the notebook and 0.71 in production A team in Noida shipped a churn model with a cross-validated ROC-AUC of 0.94. In production it scored 0.71. The bug was three lines at the top of the notebook: ```python scaler = StandardScaler() X_scaled = scaler.fit_transform(X) # <- fitted on ALL the data X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(X_scaled, y, test_size=0.2) ``` The scaler computed its mean and standard deviation from the entire dataset, including the rows that later became the test set. Every "held-out" row had already contributed to the transformation applied to it. The same happened during cross-validation — each fold's validation data had leaked into the scaling. The inflation was 0.23 AUC. Not a rounding error; the difference between a model worth deploying and one that was not. The fix is not "remember to scale after splitting". It is to make the mistake structurally impossible, and that is what pipelines are for. ##### What a pipeline is A `Pipeline` chains transformers and a final estimator into one object that behaves like a single model. ```python from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression pipe = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)), ]) pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) # each step's fit_transform, then the model's fit pipe.predict(X_test) # each step's transform, then the model's predict pipe.score(X_test, y_test) ``` The mechanics that matter: on `fit`, every step runs `fit_transform` **using only the data it is given**. On `predict`, every step runs `transform` using the parameters learned during fit. The scaler's mean can never come from data the model has not trained on. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph fit["pipe.fit X_train"] A[X_train] --> B[Imputer.fit_transform
learns the median] B --> C[Scaler.fit_transform
learns mean and std] C --> D[Model.fit] end subgraph predict["pipe.predict X_test"] E[X_test] --> F[Imputer.transform
uses TRAIN median] F --> G[Scaler.transform
uses TRAIN mean and std] G --> H[Model.predict] end ``` Four benefits follow from that one design: - **Leakage prevention** — the Noida bug becomes impossible to write. - **Correct cross-validation** — preprocessing is refitted inside every fold. - **One object to deploy** — save the pipeline and the whole transformation travels with the model. - **Tunable preprocessing** — grid search can optimise the imputation strategy alongside the model's parameters. ##### ColumnTransformer for mixed data Real datasets have numeric and categorical columns needing different treatment. `ColumnTransformer` applies different pipelines to different columns. ```python import pandas as pd from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer num_cols = ["age", "income_inr", "tenure_months", "monthly_charges"] cat_cols = ["city", "plan_type", "payment_method"] numeric_pipe = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True)), ("scale", StandardScaler()), ]) categorical_pipe = Pipeline([ ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="constant", fill_value="__missing__")), ("encode", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore", min_frequency=0.01, sparse_output=False)), ]) preprocess = ColumnTransformer( transformers=[ ("num", numeric_pipe, num_cols), ("cat", categorical_pipe, cat_cols), ], remainder="drop", # explicitly drop anything not listed verbose_feature_names_out=False, ) full_pipe = Pipeline([ ("prep", preprocess), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, class_weight="balanced")), ]) full_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) ``` Three arguments deserve attention. **`handle_unknown="ignore"`** is essential. In production you will receive a `city` value that was not in training. Without this, the encoder raises an exception and your API returns a 500. With it, the unseen category becomes all-zeros and the prediction proceeds. **`add_indicator=True`** on the imputer adds a binary column marking which values were missing. Missingness is frequently informative — a customer who did not provide income may differ systematically from one who did. **`remainder="drop"`** is explicit about columns you did not list. The alternative, `"passthrough"`, silently includes them unprocessed, which is how customer IDs end up as model features. Selecting columns by dtype rather than by name keeps the code robust as the schema changes: ```python from sklearn.compose import make_column_selector preprocess = ColumnTransformer([ ("num", numeric_pipe, make_column_selector(dtype_include="number")), ("cat", categorical_pipe, make_column_selector(dtype_include=object)), ]) ``` Inspecting what came out: ```python full_pipe.fit(X_train, y_train) names = full_pipe.named_steps["prep"].get_feature_names_out() print(len(names), names[:10]) coefs = pd.Series(full_pipe.named_steps["model"].coef_[0], index=names) print(coefs.abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10)) ``` `get_feature_names_out()` is what lets you map coefficients back to meaningful names after one-hot encoding has multiplied your columns. ##### Demonstrating the leakage Do not take the 0.23 AUC gap on faith — reproduce it. ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score, StratifiedKFold from sklearn.feature_selection import SelectKBest, f_classif cv = StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42) # WRONG: preprocessing before cross-validation X_leaky = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) X_leaky = SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20).fit_transform(X_leaky, y) # worse: uses y! leaky = cross_val_score(LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000), X_leaky, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc") # CORRECT: everything inside the pipeline clean_pipe = Pipeline([ ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("select", SelectKBest(f_classif, k=20)), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)), ]) clean = cross_val_score(clean_pipe, X, y, cv=cv, scoring="roc_auc") print(f"leaky: {leaky.mean():.4f} ± {leaky.std():.4f}") print(f"clean: {clean.mean():.4f} ± {clean.std():.4f}") print(f"inflation: {leaky.mean() - clean.mean():.4f}") ``` Feature selection is the most dramatic case. `SelectKBest` uses the target to choose features, so selecting before cross-validation means every fold's "held-out" data helped decide which features the model would see. On wide datasets this can inflate scores by 0.1 AUC or more, and on pure noise it can produce apparent skill from nothing. The leakage sources ranked by how often they appear in beginner code: | Source | Severity | Fix | |---|---|---| | Scaling before split | Moderate | Put the scaler in the pipeline | | Imputing with the full dataset's median | Moderate | Imputer in the pipeline | | Feature selection before CV | **Severe** | Selector in the pipeline | | Target encoding without cross-fitting | **Severe** | Out-of-fold encoding | | Resampling (SMOTE) before split | Severe | Use `imblearn.Pipeline` | | Duplicate rows across train and test | Severe | Deduplicate before splitting | | Time-series with random splits | Severe | `TimeSeriesSplit` | Note that `imblearn` provides its own `Pipeline` because scikit-learn's does not apply resampling correctly — resampling must happen on training folds only, never on validation data. ##### Hyperparameter search over the whole pipeline Because a pipeline is a single estimator, grid search can tune preprocessing and model parameters together. The syntax uses `stepname__parameter` with a double underscore. ```python from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, RandomizedSearchCV from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier param_grid = { "prep__num__impute__strategy": ["mean", "median"], "prep__num__scale": [StandardScaler(), RobustScaler(), "passthrough"], "model__n_estimators": [200, 500], "model__max_depth": [None, 10, 20], "model__min_samples_leaf": [1, 5, 10], } search = GridSearchCV( Pipeline([("prep", preprocess), ("model", RandomForestClassifier(random_state=42))]), param_grid, cv=StratifiedKFold(5, shuffle=True, random_state=42), scoring="roc_auc", n_jobs=-1, refit=True, # refits the best config on all training data verbose=1, ) search.fit(X_train, y_train) print("best params:", search.best_params_) print(f"best CV AUC: {search.best_score_:.4f}") print(f"test AUC: {search.score(X_test, y_test):.4f}") results = pd.DataFrame(search.cv_results_) print(results.nlargest(5, "mean_test_score")[ ["mean_test_score", "std_test_score", "params"]]) ``` Note `"prep__num__scale": [..., "passthrough"]` — you can tune whether a step runs at all, which is a neat way to test whether scaling actually helps. **Grid search is exhaustive and scales terribly.** That grid is 2 × 3 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 108 combinations × 5 folds = 540 fits. Add two more parameters and it becomes unusable. `RandomizedSearchCV` samples a fixed number of combinations from distributions instead, and Bergstra & Bengio showed it finds comparable results in far fewer trials when only some parameters matter: ```python from scipy.stats import randint, uniform param_dist = { "model__n_estimators": randint(100, 800), "model__max_depth": [None] + list(range(5, 40, 5)), "model__min_samples_leaf": randint(1, 20), "model__max_features": uniform(0.1, 0.9), } search = RandomizedSearchCV(pipe, param_dist, n_iter=50, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc", random_state=42, n_jobs=-1) ``` Two disciplines that keep search honest. Use a **nested** approach or a final untouched test set — `best_score_` is optimistically biased because you selected on it across many configurations. And search on the **training set only**, reporting the final number on data the search never saw. ##### Saving and loading ```python import joblib from pathlib import Path Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True) joblib.dump(search.best_estimator_, "models/churn_pipeline_v3.joblib", compress=3) # Later, in a different process entirely model = joblib.load("models/churn_pipeline_v3.joblib") prediction = model.predict_proba(new_customer_df)[:, 1] ``` The saved object contains everything — imputer medians, scaler statistics, encoder categories, and the trained model. A new row of raw data goes in, a prediction comes out, with no risk of the preprocessing being applied differently than it was in training. That is the deployment argument for pipelines, and it is as important as the leakage argument. Practical requirements for this to work reliably: ```python import sklearn, json, datetime metadata = { "sklearn_version": sklearn.__version__, # MUST match on load "trained_at": datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(), "features": list(X_train.columns), # column order matters "cv_auc": round(search.best_score_, 4), "test_auc": round(search.score(X_test, y_test), 4), "params": {k: str(v) for k, v in search.best_params_.items()}, } Path("models/churn_pipeline_v3.json").write_text(json.dumps(metadata, indent=2)) ``` Version mismatches between the saving and loading environment produce warnings at best and silently wrong behaviour at worst — pin `scikit-learn` in your requirements and record the version alongside the model. A security note worth knowing: `joblib` uses pickle, which executes code on load. **Never load a model file from an untrusted source.** ##### Advanced pipeline components ```python from sklearn.pipeline import FeatureUnion from sklearn.preprocessing import FunctionTransformer # Custom transformation as a pipeline step def add_ratios(df): df = df.copy() df["charges_per_month"] = df["total_charges"] / df["tenure_months"].clip(lower=1) df["income_per_person"] = df["income_inr"] / df["household_size"].clip(lower=1) return df pipe = Pipeline([ ("features", FunctionTransformer(add_ratios, validate=False)), ("prep", preprocess), ("model", LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000)), ]) # Caching expensive steps during grid search from tempfile import mkdtemp pipe = Pipeline([...], memory=mkdtemp()) # reuses fitted transformers across the grid ``` `memory=` is genuinely useful when a preprocessing step is expensive — grid search will fit it once per unique configuration rather than once per combination. For anything beyond a simple function, write a custom transformer: ```python from sklearn.base import BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin class OutlierCapper(BaseEstimator, TransformerMixin): def __init__(self, lower=0.01, upper=0.99): self.lower, self.upper = lower, upper def fit(self, X, y=None): self.bounds_ = X.quantile([self.lower, self.upper]) # learned from TRAIN only return self def transform(self, X): return X.clip(self.bounds_.iloc[0], self.bounds_.iloc[1], axis=1) ``` The trailing underscore on `bounds_` follows the scikit-learn convention marking a learned attribute — and note that the quantiles are computed in `fit`, so the test set is capped using training bounds rather than its own. ##### Common mistakes - Fitting a scaler, imputer or encoder before the train/test split. - Feature selection outside the pipeline — the worst leakage source. - Using sklearn's `Pipeline` for SMOTE instead of `imblearn`'s. - `remainder="passthrough"` letting IDs into the feature set. - No `handle_unknown="ignore"`, so an unseen category crashes production. - Reporting `best_score_` from grid search as the final performance. - Exhaustive grid search over six parameters. - Saving the model without recording the scikit-learn version. - Saving only the estimator and re-implementing preprocessing at serving time. - Loading a pickled model from an untrusted source. ##### Hands-on Build a pipeline with a `ColumnTransformer` that median-imputes and scales numeric columns while constant-imputing and one-hot encoding categoricals, ending in a classifier. Verify it works end to end, then inspect `get_feature_names_out()` and map the model coefficients back to readable names. Tune it with `GridSearchCV`, including at least one preprocessing parameter in the grid, and report both the cross-validated score and the untouched test score so you can see the optimism gap. For the mini-project, refactor an earlier end-to-end model into a single pipeline handling all preprocessing, tuned with a randomised search, and saved with `joblib` alongside a JSON metadata file recording versions, features, parameters and scores. Then write a small `predict.py` that loads the saved pipeline and scores a raw CSV — proving the deployment story works. Include an unseen categorical value in that CSV to confirm `handle_unknown="ignore"` behaves as intended. For the assignment, demonstrate data leakage empirically. Scale (and ideally also select features) outside the pipeline, cross-validate, and record the score. Then do the same inside a pipeline and record it again. Report the difference and explain exactly which information crossed the boundary and why it inflated the estimate. Doing this on your own data, with your own numbers, is what makes the lesson permanent. ##### Key takeaways - A pipeline refits every preprocessing step on each fold's training data, which makes the most common leakage bug impossible. - `ColumnTransformer` applies different treatment to numeric and categorical columns within one leakage-safe object. - Feature selection and target encoding outside the pipeline cause the most severe inflation — put them inside. - Tune preprocessing and model parameters together with `step__param` syntax, and prefer randomised search over exhaustive grids. - Save the whole pipeline with `joblib` plus version metadata; the transformations must travel with the model.
practical_task_reference: Build a pipeline with a ColumnTransformer that scales numeric and one-hot encodes categorical columns, ends in a classifier, and tune it with GridSearchCV using cross-validation.
mini_project_reference: Refactor an earlier end-to-end model into a single scikit-learn pipeline that handles all preprocessing, is tuned with grid search, and is saved to disk with joblib for reuse.
assignment_reference: Demonstrate data leakage by scaling before vs inside a pipeline and report the difference in cross-validated scores with an explanation.
